title: Panna Cotta
subtitle: Italian set cream dessert with strawberry coulis
excerpt: The understated Italian dessert: sweetened double cream barely set with gelatine and turned out to a trembling wobble. Plain to look at, remarkable to eat. Served with a sharp strawberry or raspberry coulis that cuts through the richness.

recipe.sourceNotes: Panna cotta (cooked cream) is a Piedmontese dessert of unclear but relatively recent origin; food historians place it in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, though it was not widely documented until the latter half of the twentieth century. The defining characteristic is the texture: unlike a blancmange or traditional set cream, panna cotta should be barely set, trembling at the slightest touch, almost liquid in the centre. This requires the minimum gelatine needed to hold the shape; too much and the result is rubbery. The vanilla version with red fruit coulis is the most widely made. The cream must be warmed, not boiled; boiling can prevent the gelatine from setting properly and drives off the cream's delicate flavour.

content.text: Use the minimum amount of gelatine: the panna cotta should wobble alarmingly when the mould is nudged. Test by chilling a teaspoon of the mixture: if it sets firm after 10 minutes it needs more cream, not less gelatine. The cream must be warm (not boiling) when you add the soaked gelatine: too hot and it will not set; too cold and the gelatine will not dissolve.

items.preparation: platinum strength; soaked in cold water for 5 minutes

content.text: Warm the cream, milk, and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar has dissolved and the mixture is hot but not boiling (about 80°C). Remove from the heat. Squeeze out the soaked gelatine leaves and add to the hot cream, stirring until completely dissolved. Add the vanilla. Strain through a fine sieve.

Lightly oil 6 ramekins or dariole moulds with a neutral oil. Pour in the cream mixture. Leave to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours until set. Meanwhile, make the coulis: blend the strawberries with the sugar and lemon juice until smooth. Pass through a sieve. Refrigerate.

To serve, run a small palette knife around the edge of each mould. Place a plate on top and invert quickly. The panna cotta should slide out cleanly; if it does not, dip the mould briefly in warm water and try again. Spoon the strawberry coulis around each.
